**The Weight of a Name**

There was a time when names were not just labels but promises. My grandmother used to say that the first word spoken into a child’s life was a seed—if planted with care, it would grow into something strong; if whispered in haste, it might wither before it took root. She was a woman who believed in the power of words, who carried a name that had been passed down through generations like a sacred artifact. *Mira*, she would tell me, was not just a sound but a legacy—a flicker of light in the dark.

I never knew my grandfather. He died before I was born, and the stories about him were few, scattered like crumbs from a feast long over. But his name lived on in the way my grandmother’s hands trembled when she spoke of him, in the way she would pause before saying it, as if the syllables themselves were heavy with something unsaid. *Vishnu*, she would murmur, and her voice would soften, as if the name itself was a prayer.

I was named after him.

It wasn’t a choice, not really. My parents had argued about it for months—*What if she doesn’t like it? What if it sounds too foreign? What if it’s too much?* But in the end, they settled on it because it was simple. Because it was his. Because, as my mother put it, *"It’s a name with weight."*

I never understood what that meant until I was older, until I stood in front of a mirror and said it aloud: *Vishnu Mira*. The way it rolled off my tongue, the way it felt like two halves of a whole. But other people didn’t always say it right. Teachers mispronounced it. Strangers butchered it. Once, a boy in my class laughed and called me *"Vishnu the Fish"* because he thought it sounded like a cartoon character. I didn’t know how to explain that it wasn’t a joke—it was a name, a piece of my grandfather, a thread connecting me to something bigger than myself.

I started to hate it.

Not the name itself, but the way it made me feel—like I was carrying something too heavy, something that didn’t quite fit. I wanted to be like the other girls in my class, with names that were easy, names that didn’t carry the ghost of a man I’d never met. So I began to shorten it. *Vish* became *Vee*, *Mira* became *Mira* (because that part was fine), and eventually, just *Vee*. It was easier. It was mine.

But then, one day, I found a letter.

It was tucked inside an old album, yellowed with age, the paper brittle under my fingers. My grandmother had written it to my grandfather, though I couldn’t read the words—she had kept it in Hindi, and I had never learned. But the envelope was addressed to him in my grandmother’s looping script, and the postmark was from a town I had never heard of. I held it to my chest, my heart pounding. *What if this changes everything?*

I took it to my mother.

She read it slowly, her fingers tracing the words as if she were reading them for the first time. Then she looked up at me, her eyes wet. *"This was the last letter he ever wrote her,"* she said. *"He died before she could answer it."*

I didn’t understand. *"But why didn’t she tell me?"*

She exhaled, her breath shaky. *"Because some things are too heavy to carry alone."*

The letter was a confession. Not of love—though there was love there, tangled with something else—but of fear. He had written about the weight of his name, how it had been a burden his whole life, how he had wanted to change it, to be something else. But his parents had refused. *"A name is not just a name,"* his father had said. *"It is a promise."*

And so, my grandfather had lived with that promise, with the knowledge that he would always be Vishnu, no matter what he wanted.

I read the letter again, this time letting the words sink in. The ink was faded, but the meaning was clear: *I am not just a name. I am not just a burden.*

That night, I stood in front of the mirror and said it again—*Vishnu Mira*—and this time, I didn’t hate it. I felt it, the weight of it, the history, the love, the fear. And for the first time, I understood that names weren’t just words. They were stories. They were legacies. They were the echoes of people who had come before us, whispering through the air, asking us to carry them forward.

I didn’t change it.

I just learned to carry it better.
